Lessons.Title: What Makes Sense in the Problem?
ExplanationParagraphs: Original 2021 Grade3 Unit6 Lesson14 addresses time/volume contextual reasoning and three-digit addition. Owner-device source teacher lesson.html SHA256 29f3fe72db2c7fad902de42e302d473821b6df306e5439a9a3254ccfb2e93429 and preparation.html SHA256 9c3e8c499525bbeeea6df5e23e8f062581843525b03cfbc61adec339c4e1fa66 read together with all three original student-facing sections. The separate original Student Task Statements PDF and source fair/stand photographs were not individually inspected or copied; publisher teacher-only Cool-down A Show at the Carnival remains inaccessible.

Warm-up Number Talk Give and Take (10minutes) has precisely FOUR original expressions: 306+199=505;318+297=615;275+325=600;275+329=604. Students may compensate one addend by moving1,2 or3 to nearby hundreds, and should describe the mental strategy, not just supply values.

Activity1 Carnival Time Number Choice (20min), ORIGINAL pupil material has EXACTLY THREE narrative problems with deliberately BLANK quantities, completed by groups of THREE (one member initially responsible for one situation). Story 1: Clare waits for Tyler to finish Ferris wheel; pupils choose Tyler's departure and return times and find waiting duration. Story 2: after Tyler returns, both join roller coaster line and WAIT for a student-chosen number of minutes; original arrival-on-ride clock time is chosen by pupil; determine when they joined queue. Story 3: Clare and Tyler arrived at carnival at chosen time, then after pupil-chosen number of minutes bought lemonade; determine lemonade-break time. These blanks admit MANY correct choices; teacher checks realistic chronological order and constraints, not one fixed answer.

Activity1 pupils DISCUSS selected numbers with group and justify plausibility. The source does not assert ferris-wheel ride duration, wait time or arrival time as fixed; do not put teacher examples into answer keys. After each pupil picks values, group solves ALL THREE stories using elapsed-minute rules. Original source carnival/Ferris-wheel photo third-party art not republished.

Activity2 Lemonade Break (15minutes): original stand story states EXACT quantities: produces132 liters per day; at Clare/Tyler's visit90 liters REMAIN; at end of day56 liters REMAIN, packed into FOUR-LITER JUGS. Student is asked to WRITE a plausible mathematical QUESTION matching the GIVEN mathematical work, rather than to solve a newly invented closed-form story. First printed source computation132−90=42 liters. Example valid original-context question: 'How many liters were used before Clare and Tyler stopped by?' The source also displays a tape DIAGRAM with FOURTEEN segments each labelled4 and whole56, representing56÷4=14 jugs. That source diagram data is evidenced in local file image alt, not pixel inspected. Example matching question: 'How many full 4-liter jugs can be filled with56 liters at the end?' More than one equivalent question wording can be valid; grade linkage to source computations.

Another independent mathematical consequence from source data is90−56=34 liters removed after their visit, but that is NOT the first printed work and must not be represented as the original teacher's supplied first expression. Its numerical validity does not justify replacing the two published given-work prompts. Source Lesson Synthesis revisits Ferris wheel and asks children to GENERATE their OWN multiplication/division situation; teacher sample examples include4-minute rides repeated5 times,12 cars each holding2 people, or6 tickets per person for42 tickets. These are EXAMPLES, not uniquely required source final exercise answers.

Correct source modelling balances arithmetic accuracy, units, and real-world narrative. Original illustrated tape geometry not pixel-comparable, publisher student PDF and teacher-only Cool-down unreviewed, tests written not run, Stage D not started and no academic sign-off or production release.

KeyConcepts.Title: Compensate addends
KeyConcepts.Definition: Shift a small amount from one addend to the other while keeping total constant.

KeyConcepts.Title: Choose sensible missing times
KeyConcepts.Definition: Source deliberately leaves start/end/wait numbers to the learners.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Elapsed duration must be nonnegative, chronological and plausible for context.
KeyConcepts.Example: Source roller coaster wait and arrival time have many valid responses.

KeyConcepts.Title: Ask matching numerical work questions
KeyConcepts.Definition: Given arithmetic or tape diagram can represent different phrasings grounded in context.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Map quantities and operation to correct original source story.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equal-sized jug diagram
KeyConcepts.Definition: 14 equal pieces of4 liters sum to56 liters.
KeyConcepts.Example: The original tape source 14 equal segments of4 each total56.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source lemonade work one
WorkedExamples.Question: Which real-world question corresponds to132−90=42?
WorkedExamples.Method: Subtract remainder at visit from daily starting amount.
WorkedExamples.Answer: How much lemonade was sold or consumed before their visit? 42L.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source 14-by-4 tape diagram
WorkedExamples.Question: Which question corresponds to total56 liters divided into4-liter jugs?
WorkedExamples.Answer: 14 jugs; ask how many jugs can be filled.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Grade one chosen carnival time as the only acceptable original answer.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Original explicitly asks pupils to insert their own meaningful quantities.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Verify consistency and chronological plausibility instead.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Confuse42 liters with56 liters or14 jugs.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: 42 is sold/used before the visit;56 is remaining at end;14 counts four-liter jugs.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Connect each answer to correct quantity/unit.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Require one exact question wording for given132−90=42.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Source asks students to invent contextual question.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Accept any wording whose numbers and operation represent the same source work.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: 34 is an inference but not original provided equal-groups tape work.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Preserve fourteen groups of4 with total56.

SummaryPoints: Original Carnival Time: THREE student-chosen-number stories in groups of THREE; all open, realistic, chronological.
Source Lemonade daily132L, at visit90L, end56L; first supplied expression132−90=42.
Source tape diagram14 equal parts ×4L=56L, hence14 jugs; pupils WRITE matching questions.
Original publisher images/PDF/gated Cool-down, tests and Stage D unverified.
